how: A member proposes using existing red while another reports already placing there.
Flag calls recruit participants for starting, reinforcement and later repair.
A participant answers a heart invitation with a bare report of placing a red pixel.
Participants work out the flag and dispute its star and the addition of words.
Participants report painting at a proposed new site and completing the star.
Coordinates and image templates organize placing without demonstrating universal agreement.
Members discuss spare accounts, request an overnight script and circulate its link.
Complaints about flooding produce requests for a sticky and moderation directing posts to it.
Participants prioritize defending held ground and correcting pixels before further design work.
Friendly work is misidentified and outdated bots damage it, but neither exchange establishes an agreed change abandoned because keepers were not told.
A reply corrects a defender who mistakes work on the shared heart for hostile expansion.
Members apologize for displacement and ask their own placers to leave the Greek flag alone.
Members negotiate a truce and later announce an agreement for the shared heart.
Participants seek reciprocal defense and explicitly offer protection in exchange for leaving a flag.
The shared heart and closing credits present collaboration between flags and named allies.
A heart proposal reports permission to place on another work.
Reported permission supports a hosting claim but does not establish a durable rule or every host member's consent.
A participant reports taking a reciprocal defense proposal to another room.
A complaint receives a disclaimer that one participant cannot stop every free placer.
The evidenced disclaimer answers a complaint rather than following an agreement, so it lies outside the revised arrow's explicit bound.
Attack proposals target occupied space and named rivals, while some members refuse them.
An edited battle report combines a victory claim with a proposed counterattack.
A member explicitly imports political grievances into rejection of the shared heart.
Political grievance is explicit in a heart dispute, but the cited attack proposals do not themselves name inherited rivalry as their reason.
Members describe too few placers, insufficient discipline and nowhere usable to move.
Loss prompts proposals for new coordinates and reports of moving aside from stronger opponents.
Members celebrate the completed heart, praise its appearance and credit helpers.
The closing account preserves a timelapse, final work and named contributors.
After closure participants wish for another event and invite others to another canvas.
Wishes and invitations show proposed continuation but do not demonstrate sustained collective uptake.
A postclosure reply corrects the prediction that the flag would be erased by asserting its survival in the final canvas.
A survival correction supports the element's smallest form but not organized archive cleanup or control of the historical account.
April Fools framing and mock political language turn canvas activity into occasion-specific joking.
National symbolism and opposing political interpretations coexist with the shared heart.
An explicit private poll places this episode on the decided-order side rather than contradicting the model's crossroom frequency claim.
A coordinate invitation receives a report of placing a black pixel at the requested location.
A proposal and an already-placing reply show distributed starts rather than a single observed starter followed by recruitment.
Keeping and design overlap because participants defend the flag while postponing star corrections and working on the heart.
Defense and negotiation coexist, but adjacent discussion of different opponents cannot establish that erosion by a particular neighbor caused talks with that neighbor.
A peace request receives an explicit agreement and a promise to watch for renewed intrusions.
A request for automation during sleep receives a script link.
A question about completing the star receives celebration of success and a move toward the joint heart.
Credits, final image and timelapse occur together in a closing post, which does not establish that celebration caused recording.
A timelapse and a later canvas invitation are present, but their sequence does not establish that recording generated continuation.
Scarcity can favor relocation but can also make moving impracticable when coordination or usable ground is lacking.
A circulated template does not establish settlement when members still demand one plan and correct the star.
A heart call receives a bare red-pixel report without a reason or reciprocal request.
A bare refusal limits any categorical inference that declining must supply a reason, without testing the model's crossroom frequency.
Requests for help and complaints about its absence do not by themselves establish that outsiders sent the requested pixels.
A truce offer makes defense conditional on leaving the flag, and the reply asks that promised help be communicated.
Conditional promises and requests establish proposed reciprocity rather than the delivery of protection.
A proposal for a room mark receives a suggestion to cover another flag.
An attack proposal receives refusals citing an existing site and the opponent's superior automated capacity.
A separate bare refusal is a local exception to reason-giving, not a disproof of a crossroom tendency.
A participant explicitly proposes the heart instead of attacking, tying cooperation to reputation and security.
An edited report combines attack and victory talk without establishing which act produced which utterance.
Joint work and credited allies show coalition activity but do not identify common attack as the cause of its formation.
Members explicitly connect the abundance of canvas posts to demands for concentrating them in a sticky.
Members repeatedly invite participants to Discord for organizing and defense.
Invitations establish a chat route but do not expose the decisions made inside that chat.
A participant proposes private voting and screening voters to prevent a rival from raiding the poll.
A confused participant receives an explanation of timed pixel placement.
Visiting members of allied rooms offer help or inspect the flag during collaboration.
Visitors and praise support arrivals through canvas work but not lasting membership or returning lapsed subscribers.
Claims of frontpage visibility do not identify attention from creators, teams or news media.
Early proposals choose existing red ground before a documented flag loss in these exchanges.
Members generate canvas-specific jokes about the star and a protective blue pixel.
Discord invitations show another organizing venue but do not establish that a new room formed around the canvas mark.
Political disagreement and a crude reply are recorded without evidence of members policing slurs or hate symbols.
Complaints about co-opting space, refusal to move and concern for reputation make the propriety of covering others contestable.
Profanity and complaints about canvas flooding do not establish sabotage of the room's own mark.
A participant explicitly gives up for lack of help, while others describe exhaustion from placing.
Exams, sleep and time spent repeatedly placing constrain individual participation.
A hidden mobile sticky and malfunctioning participant bots do not establish faults in the canvas site's placement machinery.
Pride in both flags and an identified Greek visitor do not establish that one participant belongs to both organizing rooms.
Building red before revealing the emblem seeks contributions from placers who do not know the eventual national design.
A checkerboard fill is proposed to avoid attracting vandals before the emblem is added.
A sticky cannot concentrate discussion for a mobile participant who cannot see it.
Joint national work does not entail political unanimity among participants.
Relocation returns participants to building at new coordinates rather than ending the organizing sequence.
